title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
statement:
You are given the price of a share on each of `n` consecutive days and an integer `k`. You may complete **at most `k` transactions**, where a transaction is one buy followed later by one sell of a single share.

You can hold at most one share at a time: you must sell the share you hold before buying again. You may sell on the same day you bought only if it makes no difference (profit 0), and you are never forced to trade.

Print the maximum total profit you can make. If no profitable trade exists, print `0`.

**Follow-up:** This generalises the one-transaction and two-transaction versions of the problem. Explain the DP table you would fill (state, transitions) and how to shrink it to O(k) memory. What changes when `k` is at least `n / 2`?
inputFormat:
The first line contains two integers `k` and `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers, the prices on days `0` to `n - 1`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the maximum profit.

examples.explanation: Buy at 1 and sell at 8 (profit 7), then buy at 3 and sell at 9 (profit 6): total 13. Splitting into 1→5, 2→8 and 3→9 would need three transactions.
Prices only fall, so the best choice is to make no transaction.
Three transactions are allowed: 2→4 (2), 1→7 (6) and 5→9 (4), for a total of 12.

hints: Think of the state after processing each day: how many transactions you have started and whether you are currently holding a share.
Let buy[j] be the best balance while holding a share during your j-th transaction, and sell[j] the best balance after completing j transactions. Update both for each new price.
If k ≥ n / 2 the limit never binds, and the answer is simply the sum of all positive day-to-day price increases.
